Can a Dental Implant Feel Too High Even If It Looks Fine?

Written By

Dental Implants Team

Introduction

Many patients who have received a dental implant are surprised to find that days or even weeks after treatment, something feels slightly off — specifically, that the implant crown feels too high when they bite down. This is a more common concern than you might expect, and it often prompts people to search online for reassurance.

What makes this situation particularly confusing is that the implant may look perfectly normal in the mirror. There is no visible swelling, no obvious misalignment, and the crown appears to match the surrounding teeth. Yet the sensation when chewing or closing the mouth can feel noticeably different or slightly elevated.

Understanding why a dental implant crown can feel too high — even when it appears visually correct — is important for patient reassurance and oral health. This article explains the dental science behind this experience, what it might mean, when it is worth monitoring at home, and when a professional dental assessment may be beneficial.

Yes. A dental implant crown can feel too high due to slight discrepancies in bite alignment that are not always visible to the naked eye. Changes in surrounding tissues during healing, bite adaptation, or minor adjustments needed to the crown's occlusal surface may all contribute. A dental professional can assess and refine the fit during a follow-up appointment.

Why Does a Dental Implant Crown Sometimes Feel Too High?

When a dental implant crown is placed, the goal is to achieve a natural, balanced bite across all teeth. This is referred to clinically as occlusion — the way the upper and lower teeth meet when you close your mouth. Even a fraction of a millimetre of additional height on the crown can be noticeable, because the teeth and jaw are remarkably sensitive to changes in bite.

There are several reasons why this might occur:

  • Healing tissue changes: In the weeks following implant crown placement, the surrounding gum tissue may settle slightly, altering how the crown sits relative to adjacent teeth.
  • Temporary anaesthetic effects: Shortly after a fitting appointment, the numbness from local anaesthetic can make it difficult to assess bite accurately. Once sensation returns, patients sometimes notice the bite feels different.
  • Initial bite adaptation: The jaw naturally adapts to new restorations, but this process can take time. What feels elevated at first may gradually feel more natural as surrounding muscles adjust.
  • Occlusal adjustment required: In some cases, a minor adjustment to the crown's biting surface is genuinely needed to achieve the correct occlusal balance.

None of these scenarios is cause for alarm, but they are all worth discussing with your dental professional if the sensation persists.

The Dental Science Behind Bite Sensitivity and Implant Crowns

Understanding why even a tiny height discrepancy can feel so pronounced requires a brief look at how the teeth and jaw work together.

Natural teeth are held in place by the periodontal ligament — a thin layer of connective tissue between the tooth root and the jawbone. This ligament acts as a sophisticated pressure sensor, providing feedback about the forces placed on a tooth during biting and chewing. It effectively tells the brain how much pressure is being applied and helps the jaw adjust accordingly.

Dental implants, by contrast, are osseointegrated — meaning the titanium implant post bonds directly with the jawbone without a periodontal ligament. This means the implant does not have the same natural shock-absorbing or pressure-sensing mechanism. As a result, even very minor height differences in the crown can feel more pronounced than they might with a natural tooth.

This is not a flaw in implant design — it is simply a biological difference. It does mean, however, that bite calibration during the crown fitting process is particularly important, and that some patients may require a brief follow-up adjustment to achieve optimal comfort.

If you are exploring single tooth implant treatment in London, understanding this aspect of care may help set realistic expectations about the fitting and adjustment process.

Signs That Your Implant Crown May Need a Bite Adjustment

Most patients can tell when something does not feel quite right, even if they struggle to describe it precisely. The following signs may suggest that a bite adjustment could be beneficial:

  • A consistent clicking or tapping sensation when teeth come together, specifically at the implant site
  • Jaw muscle tension or mild soreness, particularly along the jaw or temple area after chewing
  • Discomfort when biting on firmer foods, even if there is no sharp pain
  • A feeling that the implant crown is the first tooth to make contact when closing the mouth
  • Slight sensitivity around the implant site that does not resolve after the initial healing period

It is important to note that these sensations, when mild and transient, may simply be part of the natural adaptation period following crown placement. However, if any of these signs are persistent or worsening rather than improving over time, it is appropriate to arrange a review with your dental professional.

Patients who are unsure whether their symptoms reflect crown height, bite pattern, or adaptation can also compare these signs with guidance on why an implant may feel different when you bite.

What Happens During a Bite Adjustment Appointment?

A bite adjustment for a dental implant crown is typically a straightforward, non-invasive procedure. Your dental professional will ask you to bite down on a thin piece of articulating paper — a specially treated paper that leaves coloured marks on the teeth to indicate where biting pressure is concentrated. This provides a precise visual guide to where the crown may be making early or excessive contact.

Using a fine dental drill or polishing instrument, the dental professional can then selectively reduce the biting surface of the crown by a very small amount — often just fractions of a millimetre — to achieve a more balanced occlusion. This process is repeated and checked until the bite feels comfortable and pressure is evenly distributed.

In most cases, this adjustment requires no anaesthetic and takes only a few minutes. It does not damage or weaken the crown, and it is a normal and expected part of the implant restoration process for some patients. The crown's aesthetic appearance is generally unaffected by this type of adjustment.

When Professional Dental Assessment May Be Needed

Whilst minor bite sensitivity following crown placement is common and often self-resolving, there are certain situations where it is advisable to seek a professional dental evaluation sooner rather than later.

You may wish to contact your dental practice if you experience:

  • Persistent discomfort or pressure at the implant site lasting more than two to three weeks after fitting
  • Pain or aching in the jaw joint (TMJ) that you did not experience before the implant crown was placed
  • Visible changes around the implant, such as gum recession, redness, or swelling
  • Looseness or movement of the crown
  • A sudden change in how your bite feels after it had previously settled

It is also worth noting that a crown that is consistently too high can, over time, place excessive force on the implant and surrounding bone. Seeking a review in these circumstances is a sensible and proactive step. Dental symptoms and treatment options should always be assessed individually during a clinical examination.

Prevention and Oral Health Advice for Implant Patients

Taking an informed approach to your implant care can help reduce the likelihood of bite-related concerns and support long-term implant health.

Attend follow-up appointments: Many practices schedule a review appointment several weeks after crown placement. These are an ideal opportunity to report any bite concerns while they are easy to address.

Communicate openly at your fitting: During crown placement, when your dentist asks you to bite down and check the fit, take your time. Report any sensation of elevated height, even if it seems minor.

Maintain excellent oral hygiene: While bite adjustment relates primarily to crown fit rather than hygiene, good oral hygiene around the implant supports healthy gum tissue, which in turn contributes to stable crown positioning over time. Learn more about maintaining your implant with good oral hygiene.

Avoid very hard foods immediately after crown placement: During the initial adaptation period, being mindful of what you chew may reduce unnecessary pressure whilst the bite settles.

Report changes promptly: If you notice a shift in your bite weeks or months after a successful fitting, this is worth mentioning at your next dental appointment, even if it is mild.

Key Points to Remember

  • A dental implant crown can feel too high even when it looks visually normal, due to the absence of a periodontal ligament around the implant.
  • Even a very small height discrepancy — as little as a fraction of a millimetre — can be noticeable when biting.
  • This is a common and manageable issue that can often be resolved with a minor, non-invasive bite adjustment.
  • The sensation may also be part of natural adaptation following crown placement and may improve on its own within a few weeks.
  • Persistent discomfort, jaw muscle tension, or worsening symptoms are reasons to contact your dental practice for a review.
  • Regular follow-up appointments and open communication with your dental team are key to long-term implant comfort.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is it normal for a dental implant crown to feel high after fitting?

Yes, it is relatively common for patients to notice that a new implant crown feels slightly elevated when biting, particularly in the days immediately following fitting. This can occur because local anaesthetic during the procedure temporarily affects bite assessment, or because the surrounding tissues are still settling. In many cases the sensation improves within a few weeks. If it persists or causes discomfort, a minor bite adjustment by your dental professional can usually resolve the issue quickly and comfortably.

Can a high bite on a dental implant cause long-term problems?

If a dental implant crown remains significantly out of occlusal balance for an extended period, it may place increased stress on the implant, the surrounding bone, and the jaw joint. This does not mean that noticing a slightly high bite should cause alarm, but it is a good reason to seek a professional review rather than waiting indefinitely. Early correction of bite issues is straightforward and helps protect the long-term health and stability of the implant. Your dental professional can assess whether any adjustment is needed.

Why can I feel a high bite on an implant but not on a natural tooth?

Natural teeth are cushioned by the periodontal ligament, a thin tissue layer that absorbs pressure and provides sensory feedback. This ligament can subtly compensate for minor height variations. Dental implants integrate directly with the jawbone and do not have this ligament, meaning the sensory response to bite pressure works differently. As a result, even small discrepancies in crown height can feel more pronounced on an implant than on a natural tooth — which is why precise bite calibration is particularly important during the fitting process.

How quickly can a high bite on a dental implant be corrected?

A bite adjustment appointment is usually brief and straightforward. Using articulating paper to identify pressure points, your dental professional can selectively refine the crown's occlusal surface in a matter of minutes. No anaesthetic is typically required, and the procedure does not alter the appearance of the crown. Most patients notice an immediate improvement in bite comfort. If you have concerns about your implant crown fit, contacting your dental practice to arrange a review is the most effective first step.

Could jaw pain be related to a high dental implant crown?

Mild jaw muscle tension or discomfort following crown placement may be associated with bite imbalance, as the jaw muscles work harder to compensate for an uneven occlusal surface. This can sometimes be felt in the temples, along the jaw, or around the jaw joint (TMJ). If jaw discomfort developed after your implant crown was fitted and has not resolved, it is worth mentioning to your dental professional during a review. They can assess whether bite adjustment may help and whether any further evaluation is needed. If you are considering implant-retained dentures in London, discussing bite management as part of treatment planning can be valuable.

Can a crown feel high and wide at the same time?

Yes. In some cases, patients notice both height and shape changes together, especially in the first few weeks after placement. If this sounds familiar, you may also find it useful to read about why an implant crown can feel wider than a natural tooth.

How long does it take to adjust to a new dental implant crown?

The adaptation period varies between individuals. Some patients feel comfortable with a new implant crown almost immediately, while others may take several weeks to fully adjust as the jaw muscles and bite settle into a new pattern. Minor sensations of elevated height or slight pressure often resolve naturally within two to four weeks. If comfort is not improving, or if symptoms are increasing, a clinical review is advisable. There is no set timeframe that applies to everyone, and patient experience should always guide the decision to seek further assessment.

Conclusion

The experience of a dental implant crown feeling too high — even when it appears visually correct — is a well-recognised and manageable concern. Understanding the dental science involved, particularly the absence of a periodontal ligament around implants, helps explain why bite sensitivity can be more pronounced in these restorations than in natural teeth.

For most patients, the sensation is temporary and improves naturally as the bite adapts. When it does not, a brief, straightforward bite adjustment appointment is typically all that is needed to restore comfort and protect the long-term integrity of the implant.

The key message is not to ignore persistent bite-related discomfort. Communicating openly with your dental team and attending follow-up reviews are the most effective ways to ensure your implant crown functions comfortably and correctly.

Dental symptoms and treatment options should always be assessed individually during a clinical examination.
